scope: Korean 1A pedagogical risk matrix for L1-English and L1-German adult learners

evidenceTiers.A: Direct learner-corpus, experimental, or target-L1 error evidence.
evidenceTiers.B: Contrastive linguistic/pedagogical evidence strongly relevant to the learner group, but not a direct frequency claim.
evidenceTiers.C: Pedagogical hypothesis to validate in future learner corpus/pilot; never present as a proven group stereotype.

rules: Do not say 'English speakers always...' or 'German speakers always...'.
Use the matrix to design explanations, examples and diagnostics, not to predict an individual learner.
Tier C items require pilot evidence before becoming strong textbook claims.
Every trap must link to a repair strategy and 1A unit.

en.risk: Particle omission or replacement remains a major error class for English-speaking Korean learners.
en.evidenceNote: English lacks a comparable productive particle system; corpus research reports subject/object/topic/locative particles as 64.41% of particle errors, with replacement+omission 86.74% of particle error types.
en.pedagogy: Never teach particles once-and-done. Spiral them through noun+predicate frames and information context.

en.risk: Treating both as a single English-style subject marker or swapping them without discourse motivation.
en.evidenceNote: Learner-corpus studies document reciprocal replacement errors; topic/focus cannot be derived from English subject syntax alone.
en.pedagogy: Teach mini-context pairs: '저는...' for frame/topic vs '누가? 제가...' for focused/new subject. Delay exhaustive theory.

en.risk: Using one generic location marker because English 'at/in' does not align with Korean predicate-conditioned location marking.
en.evidenceNote: Particle-error studies report reciprocal 에/에서 replacement across proficiency.
en.pedagogy: Teach scene contrast: 학교에 가요 / 학교에 있어요 / 학교에서 공부해요 with movement/existence/action rather than translation labels.

en.risk: Interpreting subject honorification as a general extra-politeness marker.
en.evidenceNote: 2025 multi-method research found English-L1 learners associated -(으)시- with greater politeness regardless of subject type and often used it with addressee honorification.
en.pedagogy: Separate 'respecting the subject referent' from 'speaking politely to the listener'. Use person-role diagrams, not 'add 시 to be more polite'.

en.risk: Expecting politeness to be optional lexical courtesy rather than sentence-final grammar.
en.evidenceNote: English has no grammatical speech-level system comparable to Korean.
en.pedagogy: Treat sentence ending as relationship information. Keep 해요체 productive default; introduce register switching as recognition/social event.

en.risk: Repeating 저는/제가 or explicit pronouns because English clauses normally require overt subjects.
en.evidenceNote: Contrastive structural risk; future project learner-corpus pass should quantify it.
en.pedagogy: Show dialogue pairs where the first subject establishes context and subsequent Korean clauses omit it naturally.

en.risk: Transferring English SVO sequencing into Korean production.
en.evidenceNote: Basic typological contrast; not treated as a frequency claim.
en.pedagogy: Use movable noun-card chunks but keep predicate as the final anchor. Avoid metalanguage-heavy SOV lectures on day one.

en.risk: Using bare numerals because English normally does not require classifier-like counters.
en.evidenceNote: Pedagogical transfer hypothesis; validate in pilot.
en.pedagogy: Teach high-frequency lexical chunks (한 명, 한 잔, 한 개, 두 시) by task, not an exhaustive classifier table.

de.risk: Mapping Korean location/direction particles directly onto German prepositions/cases.
de.evidenceNote: Research specifically on German-speaking Korean learners reports beginner difficulty with 에/에서 semantic differentiation and proposes conceptual spatial mapping; a 2024 dissertation extends the target to 에/에서/(으)로.
de.pedagogy: Use destination/current location/action-path semantic maps. Do not teach '에 = in/an/zu' as a translation table.

de.risk: Treating 은/는, 이/가, 을/를 as equivalents of German Nominativ/Akkusativ or articles.
de.evidenceNote: Contrastive research shows Korean postpositions and German case/preposition systems divide grammatical, semantic and pragmatic work differently.
de.pedagogy: Explicit warning box: '조사 ≠ Kasusartikel'. Teach predicate frames and discourse function.

de.risk: Searching for a German case-form equivalent instead of learning Korean information structure.
de.evidenceNote: German-Korean contrastive work identifies different relationships among case, word order, topic and focus.
de.pedagogy: Use contextual contrast and answer-to-question pairs; German notes can compare information structure without claiming direct equivalence.

de.evidenceNote: German-Korean politeness research explicitly notes German du/Sie alongside broader Korean honorific systems; Korean honorification also tracks subject/object relationships and endings.
de.pedagogy: Teach two independent social maps. A German translation may use du while Korean remains 해요체, depending on relationship.

de.risk: Looking for a German pronoun/register equivalent for Korean subject honorification.
de.evidenceNote: German lacks a comparable morphogrammatical subject-honorific system; translation research emphasizes relation/status/context.
de.pedagogy: Use subject-referent diagrams and separate it from du/Sie choice.

de.risk: Overusing German clause analogies ('Korean is like a German subordinate clause') until learners misgeneralize.
de.evidenceNote: German/Korean contrastive studies show major word-order and case differences; German has multiple verb-position patterns while Korean is consistently head-final in core clause structure.
de.pedagogy: German subordinate-clause verb-final can be a temporary mnemonic only; label it explicitly as an analogy, not a rule equivalence.

de.risk: Restoring ich/du mechanically in Korean because German finite clauses usually express a subject.
de.evidenceNote: Contrastive hypothesis requiring project learner-corpus validation.
de.pedagogy: Show natural Korean dialogue where topic is set once and omitted afterward; DE translation may need explicit pronouns.

de.risk: Expecting German numeral+noun structure to transfer directly.
de.pedagogy: Teach task chunks rather than classifier taxonomy; contrast only when it helps.
